config.title: Raft consensus laboratory
config.objective: Predict when a Raft cluster can elect a leader and commit writes, and explain why it needs a majority.
config.summary: An intro video shows a write committing on a majority, a five-server simulation lets the learner fail servers and send writes, a guided walkthrough pauses during a leader failure, deep dives explain split brain and cluster sizes, and a final video connects the rules.

watch.title: How a Raft cluster commits one write
watch.blocker: not rendered yet; run `tutor video <topic> render <id>`
watch.transcript:
# How a Raft cluster commits one write

A client sends a write to the leader. The leader appends it to its log and sends it to two followers. When a majority stores the entry, the leader commits it and replies to the client.

**00:00 One write, three servers.** A Raft cluster commits a write in a fixed order. Watch one write travel.

**00:05 The leader appends, then replicates.** The client sends the write to the leader. The leader appends it to its log, then sends AppendEntries to each follower.

**00:14 A majority acknowledges.** Follower 1 stores the entry and replies. The leader and Follower 1 are two of three servers, which is a majority.

**00:23 Commit, apply, reply.** The leader marks the entry committed, applies it to its state machine, and replies to the client. Followers learn the commit on the next message.

**00:32 Why a majority.** When a majority stored the entry, any new leader has it. When only a minority stored it, the entry can be lost. So the leader waits for a majority.

Sources:

- Source distributed-consensus-source — https://example.com/distributed-consensus-source
watch.explanation: The leader replies only after a majority of servers store the entry. A minority failure cannot lose a committed write.

guided.title: How Raft replaces a failed leader
guided.blocker: not rendered yet; run `tutor video <topic> render <id>`
guided.transcript:
# How Raft replaces a failed leader

A five-server Raft cluster loses its leader. Heartbeats stop, a follower's election timeout fires, it becomes a candidate for term 2 and asks for votes. With three of five votes it becomes leader. When only two servers are alive, no candidate can reach a majority, so the cluster stops accepting writes.

**00:00 When the leader fails.** What happens when the Raft leader crashes?

**00:05 The leader sends heartbeats.** While it is alive, the leader sends heartbeats to the followers. Each heartbeat resets their election timers.

**00:14 Heartbeats stop, a timeout fires.** The leader crashes and the heartbeats stop. Election timeouts are random, so one follower times out first and becomes a candidate.

**00:24 The candidate asks for votes.** The candidate votes for itself and sends RequestVote to the others. Each server votes once per term. Three votes of five make it leader.

**00:34 A minority cannot elect.** If only two of five servers are alive, no candidate gets three votes. There is no leader, so no write commits.

Sources:

- Source distributed-consensus-source — https://example.com/distributed-consensus-source
guided.explanation: A leader rules only while a majority hears it. A new leader needs votes from a majority of all servers, so two leaders can never win the same term.
guided.alt: A five-server Raft cluster loses its leader. Heartbeats stop, a follower's election timeout fires, it becomes a candidate for term 2 and asks for votes. With three of five votes it becomes leader. When only two servers are alive, no candidate can reach a majority, so the cluster stops accepting writes.

summary_video.title: Raft in four rules
summary_video.blocker: not rendered yet; run `tutor video <topic> render <id>`
summary_video.transcript:
# Raft in four rules

A recap of Raft: the leader appends and replicates log entries, an entry commits once a majority stores it, a failed leader is replaced by an election that needs a majority of votes, and without a majority the cluster stops rather than give wrong answers.

**00:00 Raft in four rules.** Four rules connect everything you explored.

**00:05 The rules.** The leader appends and replicates entries. An entry commits once a majority stores it. A failed leader is replaced by an election. Without a majority, the cluster stops.

**00:19 Why majorities keep data safe.** A commit majority and an election majority of five always share at least one server. That server carries every committed entry into the next term.

Sources:

- Source distributed-consensus-source — https://example.com/distributed-consensus-source
summary_video.explanation: Every Raft rule uses the same majority, so any two majorities share a server, and that shared server carries the committed history forward.

scenes.heading: Three ways to acknowledge a write

deck.outline:
# Why consensus needs a majority

A short deck asks why Raft waits for a majority. The main path compares waiting for all servers, one server and a majority. Two deep dives show split brain without a majority rule and how many failures clusters of three to seven servers tolerate.

**Purpose.** Explore why Raft waits for a majority, what goes wrong without it, and how cluster size changes the failures it survives.

## Main path

### 1. Why wait for a majority?

**On screen.** Title card with "All, one, or a majority?".

**Notes.** Ask the learner what would go wrong with fewer or more acknowledgments.

### 2. Three ways to acknowledge a write

**On screen.** Numbered steps appear one at a time: Wait for all: one crash blocks every write → Wait for one: a crash can lose the write → Wait for a majority: survives crashes and stays safe.

**Notes.** Reveal the options one at a time and ask which survives a crash and stays available.

### 3. Majorities always overlap

**On screen.** Two columns, "Write acknowledged by" and "Next leader elected by", fill in pairs; verdict: S3 is in both majorities..

**Notes.** Two majorities of five share at least one server, so a new leader always meets a server with the committed entries.

**Branches.** deep dive "Split brain without a majority", deep dive "Why odd cluster sizes".

### 4. The trade-off

**On screen.** Two columns, "Majority alive" and "Majority lost", fill in pairs; verdict: Consistency over availability during a partition..

**Notes.** Raft chooses safety: without a majority it stops instead of risking two different histories.

## Deep dive: Split brain without a majority

### 1. A partition splits the cluster

**On screen.** Two columns, "Side A: S1, S2" and "Side B: S3, S4, S5", fill in pairs; verdict: Two histories: which x is true?.

**Notes.** If each side could elect a leader with any number of votes, both sides would accept different writes.

### 2. The majority rule prevents it

**On screen.** Numbered steps appear one at a time: Side A has 2 of 5 votes: no leader → Side B has 3 of 5 votes: S3 leads → Only side B commits writes.

**Notes.** With the majority rule only side B, with three of five servers, can elect a leader, so only one history exists.

## Deep dive: Why odd cluster sizes

### 1. Failures each size survives

**On screen.** Bars grow for 3 servers 1 failures, 4 servers 1 failures, 5 servers 2 failures, 6 servers 2 failures, 7 servers 3 failures.

**Notes.** A cluster of n servers survives floor of (n minus 1) over 2 failures; adding a fourth server adds no tolerance.
deck.explanation: A majority is the smallest group that any other majority must overlap, which is what keeps two leaders from deciding different histories.

checkpoints.prompt: In one sentence: why does the leader wait for a majority before it commits a write?
checkpoints.explanation: A majority stores the entry before it commits, and any later majority overlaps it, so the next leader always meets a server that has the entry.

checkpoints.prompt: The leader just crashed. What do the followers do first?

choices.text: Wait for an election timeout, then one becomes a candidate
Keep committing writes without a leader
choices.misconception: Thinks followers can commit without a leader

choices.text: Immediately crown the server with the lowest id
choices.misconception: Thinks Raft elects by server id instead of by votes after a random timeout

checkpoints.explanation: Followers notice the failure only when heartbeats stop and their election timer expires. The first to time out becomes a candidate for a new term and asks the others for votes.

checkpoints.prompt: In the simulation, fail servers and send a write until the write cannot commit. How many live servers are left then?

goal.hint: Fail three servers, press Send write, then press Step a few times.

checkpoints.explanation: With two of five servers alive there is no majority of three, so no leader can be elected and the write stays pending. Nothing wrong is committed; the cluster just waits.

checkpoints.prompt: A cluster has four servers. How many can fail while it still commits writes?

choices.misconception: Thinks half the servers is a majority
Thinks one live server can commit alone

checkpoints.explanation: A majority of four is three. With one failure three servers remain, which is a majority; with two failures only two remain, which is not.

checkpoints.prompt: Why can two leaders never win the same term in Raft?

choices.text: Each server votes once per term and a leader needs a majority
Servers with higher ids override others

choices.misconception: Thinks clients take part in elections

checkpoints.explanation: Two majorities of the same cluster overlap, and the shared server votes only once per term, so only one candidate can collect a majority in a term.

fallback.title: Distributed Consensus: the whole process
fallback.purpose: See every step before studying one.
fallback.explanation: Each step hands its result to the next one, and the last step gives the outcome the learner predicts.
